text: APIs, or Application Programming Interfaces, allow different software applications to communicate with each other. When you work with an API, you typically send an HTTP request to a server, asking for data or a specific action. The server then responds, often sending the requested information in JSON format, which is easy for computers to read and process. Most APIs require authentication, usually through an API key, to ensure only authorized users can access their services. It is also important to be aware of rate limits, which restrict how many requests you can make in a given time period to prevent overloading the server. Finally, always implement proper error handling, as network issues or invalid inputs can cause requests to fail, and your code should be able to manage these situations gracefully.
